statement: In people dependent on heroin going through supervised withdrawal, in three randomized trials from Australia, Germany and the USA (148 people, published 1985 to 2008, pooled in a Cochrane review searched to November 2015), clonidine or lofexidine compared with placebo reduced the chance of severe withdrawal, from about 59 to about 19 in 100 in the review's illustration (risk ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.57), and more people completed the withdrawal treatment, about 56 against 29 in 100 (risk ratio 1.95, 1.34 to 2.84). Both results held when the one trial at high risk of bias was left out. The medicines brought more side effects: drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth and low blood pressure, and in the newest trial 4 of 35 people stopped lofexidine because of side effects against none of 33 on placebo. Two of the three trials were in hospital, and no included trial is described as involving fentanyl. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In three trials, people coming off heroin or methadone who got clonidine or lofexidine had severe withdrawal less often than people who got a dummy pill, and more of them finished the withdrawal treatment. The medicines can make people sleepy or dizzy and lower blood pressure. The trials were small and old, and none was in people withdrawing from fentanyl.

Completion: RR 1.95 (1.34 to 2.84), 3 trials, 148 participants, moderate; 288 against 561 per 1000; without the high-risk trial RR 2.12 (1.40 to 3.19). Adverse effects not pooled: hypotension 18% against 0%, insomnia 42% against 9%, stopping for adverse effects 4 of 35 against 0 of 33 (Yu 2008); drowsiness and dizziness 7 of 16 against 0 of 15 (Batey 1987).

statement: In people dependent on heroin or methadone in supervised withdrawal (12 randomized trials of clonidine, lofexidine or guanfacine against a reducing course of methadone, in a Cochrane review searched to November 2015), the clonidine-type medicines compared with methadone were associated with similar overall withdrawal severity (standardized difference 0.13, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.49; 3 trials, 119 people), withdrawal that began and ended earlier (all 8 trials that described the time course), shorter time in treatment (standardized difference -1.07, -1.31 to -0.83; 3 trials, 310 people), and about twice as many people with low blood pressure or other side effects (151 against 79 in 1,000; risk ratio 1.92, 1.19 to 3.10; 6 trials, 464 people), an excess that was no longer statistically clear without the three trials at high risk of bias (2.02, 0.62 to 6.64). Completion did not differ clearly (risk ratio 0.85, 0.69 to 1.05; 9 trials, 659 people), but the interval still allows a meaningful advantage for methadone. In three small direct comparisons that could not be pooled, lofexidine lowered blood pressure less than clonidine. Neither approach fully relieved aches, poor sleep, low energy, chills or anxiety. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Compared with a slowly reducing course of methadone, clonidine-type medicines gave about the same overall withdrawal, but it came and went sooner, treatment was shorter, and side effects such as low blood pressure and dizziness were about twice as common. About as many people finished either way. Lofexidine lowered blood pressure less than clonidine in a few small studies. Neither approach took away all the aches, bad sleep and anxiety.

statement: In people dependent on opioids, mostly heroin, in supervised withdrawal (14 randomized trials, 750 people on buprenorphine and 615 on clonidine or lofexidine, in a Cochrane review searched to December 2016), buprenorphine compared with clonidine or lofexidine increased completion of withdrawal treatment, from about 45 to about 72 in 100 in the review's illustration (risk ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.06; 11 trials, 1,264 people), so that about one more person completed for every four treated with buprenorphine. It also lowered average withdrawal scores (standardized difference -0.43, -0.58 to -0.28; 7 trials, 902 people) and kept people in treatment longer (0.92, 0.57 to 1.27; 4 trials, 558 people), in hospital and outpatient settings alike. The number of people with any side effect did not differ detectably (risk ratio 0.93, 0.70 to 1.26; very low certainty); the kinds differed (dizziness, dry mouth and tiredness with clonidine; headache, constipation and nausea with buprenorphine), and only people on clonidine stopped because of side effects (3 small trials, not statistically clear). Two trials were stopped early for benefit, which can overstate effects, and no included trial is described as involving fentanyl. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials of people coming off opioids, mostly heroin, more people finished the withdrawal treatment with buprenorphine than with clonidine or lofexidine: about 72 in 100 against 45 in 100. Withdrawal was milder on average and people stayed longer. Side effects were about as common, but of different kinds. These trials were done before fentanyl was common.

statement: In people dependent on opioids in supervised withdrawal, mostly in hospital or prison (6 randomized trials, 436 people, in a Cochrane review searched to December 2016), buprenorphine compared with a reducing course of methadone did not detectably change completion of withdrawal treatment: about 55 against 53 in 100 in the review's illustration (risk ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.20; 5 trials, 457 people), an interval that rules out large differences but not a gain of up to about 11 completions in 100 with buprenorphine or a loss of about 5. Time in treatment did not differ clearly (2 trials, 82 people, low certainty). Withdrawal severity and side effects could not be pooled: two trials found no difference in severity, two found differences on some days in opposite directions, and three reported no significant side effects with either medicine. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: Buprenorphine and a slowly reducing course of methadone helped about the same share of people finish withdrawal treatment, about 55 and 53 in 100. There were only six small trials, mostly in hospitals or a prison, and they could not show whether withdrawal felt different with one or the other.

statement: As described in a narrative review (Angarita et al., 2016; figures second-hand, no systematic search or appraisal), in people dependent on heroin or other opioids sleep is disturbed during regular use and in the weeks after stopping: in cited sleep-laboratory studies, the first week of abstinence from heroin brought shorter sleep, less deep (slow-wave) and REM sleep, longer time to fall asleep and more waking than in healthy sleepers, and over the first three weeks time to fall asleep was still long and sleep less efficient. In methadone maintenance more than three-quarters of people reported sleep complaints and about half used illicit drugs or medicines to help them sleep; long-term opioid use was linked with pauses in breathing during sleep (signs of central sleep apnoea in 30 to 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy), and buprenorphine treatment with sleep-disordered breathing in one study of 70 patients. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A review of sleep research says that people coming off heroin sleep less and more lightly for weeks, and take longer to fall asleep. Many people on methadone also sleep badly, and long-term opioid use can cause pauses in breathing during sleep. The review did not check the studies' quality, so these are second-hand findings.
population: People with opioid use disorder (heroin; methadone or buprenorphine treatment; long-term opioid therapy), in studies cited by a narrative review
exposure: Regular opioid use and abstinence after it
comparator: Healthy sleepers or the same people at other times, as in the cited studies
outcome: Polysomnographic and self-reported sleep, sleep-disordered breathing
magnitude: Second-hand, as summarized: early abstinence from heroin with reduced total, slow-wave and REM sleep and increased sleep latency and waking (Howe et al.); prolonged sleep latency and reduced efficiency over the first three weeks (Asaad et al.); sleep complaints in more than three-quarters of people in methadone maintenance, about half using drugs or medicines to sleep; central apnoea signs in 30 to 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy.

statement: In 26 people seen in person by medical toxicologists at 50 US sites after taking loperamide, an anti-diarrhoea medicine that is an opioid (registry cases from 2010 or 2011 to 2016; intent known for 18: 12 misuse, 6 of whom had taken it to avoid opioid withdrawal, 3 attempted self-harm and 3 young children), the registry describes frequent heart-rhythm problems: a prolonged QTc interval in 10 (38.5%), ventricular dysrhythmias in 6 or 7 (the abstract and the results differ), a widened QRS in 6 (23.1%) and a heart attack in 1, as well as coma or depressed consciousness in 11 (42.3%) and slowed breathing in 5. Seventeen needed specific treatment, 4 a breathing tube, 2 a pacemaker and 1 resuscitation; none died. Everyone with a ventricular dysrhythmia whose amount was recorded had taken far more than the label allows. These are only the cases that reached a toxicologist, the amount was known for 9 of 26 and there is no comparison group, so the series cannot show how often this happens, whether any amount is safe, or that loperamide alone caused each problem. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Doctors who treat poisonings in the USA described 26 people who became ill after taking loperamide, some of them to get through opioid withdrawal: many had dangerous changes in heart rhythm, some needed a breathing tube or a pacemaker, and none died. These were only people ill enough to reach these doctors, so the study cannot say how often this happens.
population: People seen in person by medical toxicologists at 50 US sites after loperamide exposure, 2010 or 2011 to 2016 (ToxIC Registry), including people who took it to avoid opioid withdrawal
exposure: Loperamide, in the cases with heart-rhythm problems far above the label amount, sometimes with other substances (7 of 26)
outcome: Heart-rhythm problems (prolonged QTc, wide QRS, ventricular dysrhythmias), depressed consciousness and breathing, treatment needed and survival
magnitude: Prolonged QTc 10 of 26 (38.5%); ventricular dysrhythmias 6 (Results) or 7 (abstract), 5 of 6 after loperamide alone; prolonged QRS 6 (23.1%); myocardial infarction 1 (3.8%); coma or CNS depression 11 (42.3%); respiratory depression 5 of 26 (printed 15.4%; 19.2% by editors' calculation); specific toxicological treatment 17 (65%); intubation 4, pacing 2, resuscitation 1; no deaths. No denominator of people exposed; amount recorded in 9 of 26.

statement: In clients of 27 harm reduction supply sites across British Columbia, Canada, surveyed in 2018 (414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months, recruited by convenience at the sites), 314 (75.8%; editors' 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%) said they had used drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, and 198 (47.8%) more than a quarter of the time, answering one question that did not define alone (Papamihali et al., 2020). Offered a short list of reasons, with more than one allowed, the 314 most often chose that it is more convenient and comfortable to use at home (139, 44.3%; 52.7% of the 264 who gave a reason, editors' calculation), then not wanting others to know (44, 14.0%; more often under age 50 than at 50 or older, 16.9% against 5.3%) and that it is safer to be alone (30, 9.6%). Two more reasons were not on the list but were coded by the authors from written answers: having no one to use with (37, 11.7%) and not wanting to share or it being cheaper (27, 8.6%); because they could be given only in writing, their shares cannot be ranked against the listed options and may be undercounts. Written answers also included having no access to an overdose prevention site and not being allowed to use in a transition home. People who used alone more often had no regular housing (37.6% against 24.0% of those who did not use alone; adjusted odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.27, in 306 people with complete answers) and more often had used crack or cocaine in the past week (41.4% against 26.0%; 2.10, 1.15 to 3.82). They also more often reported an opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months (22.9% against 15.0%), but not significantly after adjustment (1.71, 0.79 to 3.69); both were reported by the same people at one sitting, so this is an association, not a prediction, and the survey cannot say whether using alone changes the risk of overdose. Coroners' reports cited in the paper's background, not data of this study, found that 69% of people who died of an overdose in British Columbia in 2016–2017 were using alone and that in 2019 the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths; the paper does not say how these deaths were defined or how using alone was established. People already in contact with services were surveyed, so the figures may not hold for people who use drugs and do not attend these sites. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a 2018 survey at 27 harm reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, about 3 in 4 people had used drugs alone at least once in the past week. The reason chosen most often was that using at home is easier and more comfortable; others did not want people to know or felt safer alone, and some wrote that they had no one to use with. The survey could not show whether using alone changes the risk of overdose, but coroners' reports it cites found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose in the province in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.
population: Clients of 27 harm reduction supply distribution sites in all five health regions of British Columbia, Canada, May to August 2018: 414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months (62.6% men; 34.3% not regularly housed; past-week use of opioids 70.0%, crystal methamphetamine 72.9%, crack or cocaine 37.7%, benzodiazepines 13.5%), recruited by convenience at the sites
exposure: Using drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, from one self-report item (share of the time drugs were used alone, in bands, counted as any against none; alone not defined for respondents)
comparator: Respondents who did not use alone in the past 7 days (100), for the correlates; none for the reasons
outcome: Reasons chosen from a short list (more than one allowed, with free text, from which the authors coded two further reasons), asked only of those who used alone; characteristics associated with using alone; self-reported opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months
magnitude: Used alone in the past 7 days: 314 of 414 (75.8%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%); more than 25% of the time: 198 (47.8%). Reasons (of 314): listed options: convenience and comfort at home 139 (44.3%; 52.7% of 264 giving a reason, editors' calculation), not wanting others to know 44 (14.0%), safer alone 30 (9.6%); coded by the authors from written answers: no one to use with 37 (11.7% as printed; 11.8% by editors' calculation), not wanting to share or cheaper 27 (8.6%), other reasons that could not be coded 19 (6.1%); prefer not to say 31 (9.9%), no response 19 (6.1%). Adjusted odds ratios (n = 306): no regular housing 2.27 (1.20 to 4.27); crack or cocaine 2.10 (1.15 to 3.82); opioids 1.59 (0.87 to 2.88); crystal methamphetamine 1.58 (0.86 to 2.88); opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months 1.71 (0.79 to 3.69). Naloxone kit: 67.8% of those who used alone against 66.0%. Coroners' figures cited in the background: 69% of overdose deaths in 2016–2017 involved using alone; in 2019, the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths and another residence for 26.5%.

statement: Reviews of the same death-investigation files in Maryland and Victoria identified more heroin-related deaths under their own definitions than a search of certificate text or national heroin codes. Morphine recorded instead of heroin, general drug wording and coding or registration issues contributed, but the comparisons do not validate a universal rate of deaths caused by heroin. An England and Wales projection addresses a different quantity: combined heroin/morphine deaths, not heroin misnamed as morphine. In Maryland in 2012–2015, the authors' search of the state's medical-examiner certificates found heroin named in 1,130 overdose deaths. A protocol developed by state agencies identified 2,182 using certificate text, toxicology and scene evidence: heroin on the certificate, a heroin-specific metabolite in tests, morphine with quinine, or morphine/unspecified certification together with scene evidence suggesting heroin. It excluded cases whose scene notes suggested prescription morphine. Because it retained every certificate naming heroin, it could only add heroin assignments. The 1,052 additions had morphine certified in 804 cases, no specific drug in 193 and another substance in 55. Certificates named heroin in 51.8% of protocol-defined deaths (95% interval 49.7–53.9), from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, and less often among people aged 55 or older (41.9%), women (35.1%) and non-Hispanic Black women (25.9%). The authors acknowledge that some added cases, including some of the 55, may not have been heroin-related (Horon et al., 2018). In Victoria, Australia, in 2012–2013, the authors applied their earlier heroin-attribution model to closed coronial files, using toxicology plus circumstances, clinical and pathological evidence in the context of cause of death. It selected 243 deaths, with the heroin-specific marker in 180; the remaining 63 relied on morphine findings and investigative evidence (editors' subtraction). Of those selected, 235 were toxicity deaths and eight were misadventure deaths after heroin intoxication. The paper does not say how those eight were coded; two of them carried the heroin code and appear to be among the deaths counted nationally (editors' inference from its tables). National data held 165 deaths with the heroin code, 161 inside the model-defined group and four judged coincidental by the model; 82 of the 243 lacked the heroin code, a net difference of 78 between totals. The Victorian attribution groups counted heroin named either in the cause of death or in the NCIS object-causing-death field. Of 191 toxicity deaths attributed to heroin on that basis, 37 lacked its code. The authors describe generic certification with drugs named only in the object field, morphine written as the cause with heroin only as the object, and complications listed first. They do not print a cross-tabulation separating wording issues from late registration in these groups. Of 39 deaths attributed to morphine or another opioid, 34 lacked the heroin code; all five generic-toxicity deaths lacked it. Twenty model-selected deaths had no code at all, which the authors judged most reasonably due to late initial registration and no coding assessment, not simply certificate wording. Since the study years, associated-cause toxicity codes have also become subject to revision when new information arrives, limiting application to newer statistics (Stam et al., 2019). A commentary on the Victorian study agreed that official figures under-report heroin deaths and restated, with hedges and without data of its own, the two problems the study identified: deaths certified as multiple drug toxicity appear to be systematically missed, and deaths certified as morphine toxicity would appear often to be missed (Darke, 2019). A letter replying to both argued, also without data, that definitions of drug-related death differ between jurisdictions and that a wider count, built from linked records and cohorts, should take in later deaths among older people who use or used drugs, such as from liver disease linked to hepatitis C or alcohol (Robertson et al., 2019). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, ONS counted 13,471 deaths naming heroin or morphine in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest. NPSUM's coroner reports and toxicology reports identified a further share with an ambiguous drug cause in which a consulting toxicologist implicated heroin/morphine: 29% in 2011 and 36% in 2022, the endpoint years rather than a range across all years. Applying those shares nationally, without linking individual records, projected 20,323 combined heroin/morphine deaths (95% interval 19,382–21,358), about 51% above the ONS count (editors' calculation). These intervals address sampling error in the programme's shares, not the assumption that those shares represent all cases. The median number of drugs detected in programme heroin/morphine deaths rose from four to six; detection is not proof that every drug caused death (Chen et al., 2025). A scoping review reports further comparisons second-hand. In Allegheny County in 2008–2010, heroin-involved deaths rose from 171 to 245 after review, while morphine-involved deaths fell from 132 to 41 and codeine-involved deaths from 34 to five; the decreases exceed the heroin increase, so these cannot be read as a one-for-one transfer between exclusive groups. In New York City in 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication were attributed to heroin. In SUDORS data for 38 states and Washington DC in 2018–2019, 44.2% of probable and 52.6% of suspected heroin deaths had only morphine on the certificate; enhanced definitions raised the heroin share from 80.2% to 93.3%. These primary studies were not read here, and their enhanced categories are not an independent test of true causal attribution (Gutkind et al., 2025). Heroin is rapidly converted to 6-acetylmorphine and then morphine; the specific marker may be absent after delayed death or change in stored specimens, so morphine after death can have several origins (Stam et al., 2019, describing earlier literature). National statistics also warn that a morphine mention may reflect heroin rather than direct morphine use (Garnett et al., 2026). A US medical-examiners' position paper treats 6-acetylmorphine as sufficient evidence of heroin without an attached citation; for a morphine-to-codeine ratio above one as possible evidence of heroin use it cites three empirical studies, but does not report the rule's diagnostic accuracy. Those studies were not independently read here (Davis et al., 2020). The Maryland and Victorian reference definitions were not validated against an independent causal standard, and the English and Welsh estimate is unlinked and combines two drugs. These historical findings cannot specify a current heroin-caused-death miss rate everywhere. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do official counts miss heroin deaths? In Maryland and Victoria, closer file reviews linked more deaths to heroin than certificate text or national codes did. Heroin turns into morphine in the body, and some records said morphine or mixed drugs instead. In Maryland, certificates named heroin in about 52 out of 100 deaths the fuller protocol linked to heroin. In Victoria, about 34 out of 100 model-selected deaths lacked the heroin code; a few coded as heroin were judged to involve it only by chance. The reviews used their own rules, with no independent check of whether heroin caused each death. In England and Wales, a separate estimate suggests about half as many again as counted, but it combines heroin and morphine and does not match each death across the lists. These are different comparisons, not one missing-death rate.
population: Overdose deaths investigated by Maryland's statewide medical examiner, 2012–2015; deaths in Victoria, Australia, with closed coroners' files, 2012–2013; deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales, 2011–2022; second-hand, two US county reviews (2006–2010)
exposure: Heroin named in the certificate's cause of death, or the national heroin code (ICD-10 T40.1) built from it, or a coroner's conclusion naming heroin or morphine
comparator: A fuller review of the same files with its own definition (toxicology markers, scene evidence and the coroner's findings), or, in England and Wales, a projection from a coroner-reported register with toxicology
outcome: Deaths meeting the fuller definition of a heroin-related death that the certificate or code did not attribute to heroin, and coded heroin deaths that the fuller review did not count
magnitude: Maryland 2012–2015 (Horon et al., 2018; authors' certificate-text search versus enhanced protocol): 1,130 deaths with heroin on the certificate against 2,182 by the enhanced protocol (28.6% and 55.1% of 3,957 overdose deaths, a total not defined in the paper); added 1,052: morphine certified 804, no specific drug 193, other substance 55; certificates named heroin in 51.8% (49.7–53.9) of protocol deaths, 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015); 41.9% at 55 or older, 35.1% of women, 25.9% (18.5–33.3) of non-Hispanic Black women. Reference standards unvalidated; no intervals for Victorian counts. Chen reports Wilson intervals for projections, covering sampling error only; Table 1 values used where the text differs. Commentary and letter on Stam et al. (Darke, 2019; Robertson et al., 2019): arguments only, no figures of their own.

risk_of_bias.note: Maryland and Victorian reference definitions are not independently validated causal standards. They combine toxicological markers and investigative evidence; Stam evaluates them in the context of cause of death, so it is too absolute to say no causal judgment occurred. statement: Other drugs are often detected in deaths labelled heroin overdose, but detection does not establish which substances caused a death. A 1996 narrative review, with no stated search or appraisal, selected medical-examiner and coroner series and statistics from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly published 1967–1996, leaning on the authors’ 152 deaths in New South Wales in 1992. It relays morphine as the only drug detected in 23%–48% across six series and alcohol in 29%–75% across 13, with mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL where reported. Diazepam was detected in 12% in one cited study; this is a diazepam-specific result, not sole exposure; three others reported benzodiazepines in 22%, 27% and 55%. These are second-hand findings with unknown laboratory panels and varying death definitions, not shares proved to have been caused by heroin alone or by combinations (Darke & Zador, 1996). Five cited studies reported lower blood morphine when alcohol was detected. Correlations were weak where given: −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28 in the authors’ series. A third of their series was below the laboratories’ 0.16 mg/L toxic level for people without opioid tolerance. A Michigan series published in 1977 reported 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died from other causes; the review does not establish its case-collection dates. It cites three publications about survivor comparisons without numerical results or enough detail to establish independent samples and says better living-versus-fatal comparisons would add substantially to knowledge (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). In the authors’ series 14% were classed as instant deaths and 22% took more than 3 hours; other series reported 44% beyond 2 hours and 52% beyond 3 hours. Other people were present in more than half of deaths in four studies (58%–79% where specified). The reviewers infer that combined drug toxicity explains many deaths. The editors’ limitation is that presence alone does not establish causal shares, tolerance was not measured, and delayed death is another possible explanation for low morphine. Darke and Zador do not discuss post-mortem redistribution; that separate limitation comes from toxicology literature, not their conclusions. The post-mortem result alone cannot decide the cause (Darke & Zador, 1996; Borra et al., 2026). In England and Wales in 2000, researchers reclassified1,037 accidental drug-related deaths voluntarily reported by coroners to a register of unstated completeness. They assigned 802 (77%) to direct overdose and 235 (23%) to other categories: 74 acute physical events, 112 toxicity with a medical condition, 31 traumatic accidents and 18 acute infections. Direct overdose was the default when no evidence suggested otherwise. These are recorded classifications. A ceiling for direct overdose and a floor for alternatives would be the editors’ conditional interpretation, assuming the other classifications were correct; neither is a validated bound on true causes or a measured error rate in official statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin/morphine was recorded as implicated in 424 of 802 direct overdoses and detected in 488; it was implicated in 42 of 74 acute physical events, 33 of 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition, and 11 of 18 infections. Alcohol was detected in 316 of 802 direct overdoses (39.4%), but the register recorded it only alongside other drugs. Methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses, as the sole implicated drug in 4%; sole implication does not mean no other drug was detected. Negative findings were not recorded, leaving absence versus lack of testing uncertain (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin exposure can also be missed. A review reports falling femoral-blood 6-MAM, a heroin marker, between post-mortem samples in one primary study. It also relays both higher and lower post-mortem opioid concentrations compared with samples from life, with additional timing, specimen and morphine-transformation limits (Borra et al., 2026). Another review’s table says cerebrospinal-fluid 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related cases than blood, but supplies no case counts or unique per-value primary citation; this is a second-hand testing comparison, not 46% more proven heroin-caused deaths (Leikin & Watson, 2003). The main death-series figures are historical and cannot describe current drug mixtures or yield a rate per use. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Are deaths labelled heroin overdose always caused by heroin alone? Other drugs were often found in the older studies, but that does not show which caused a death. A review relays morphine as the only drug found in 23 to 48 in 100 deaths, and alcohol in 29 to 75 in 100. Finding diazepam is different from finding any benzodiazepine, and neither means it was the only drug present. In England and Wales in 2000, researchers put 23 in 100 reported accidental drug-related deaths in categories beyond direct overdose, using the researchers’ rules. Other drugs or illnesses may matter, and heroin exposure may also be missed by tests. These records cannot tell how many deaths heroin alone caused.
population: Deaths attributed to heroin overdose by medical examiners, coroners or researchers in series from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly 1967–1996 (second-hand, Darke & Zador, 1996); 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to a national register in 2000 (Webb et al., 2003)
exposure: Heroin use, shown by morphine (and where tested 6-MAM) found after death; other drugs found or named as implicated
comparator: Morphine-only detection against co-detection; a Michigan series published 1977 comparing other-cause deaths (secondary); direct-overdose default category against alternative categories in England/Wales 2000
outcome: What else was found in deaths attributed to heroin overdose, the timing and circumstances of death, and the mechanism of death
magnitude: Secondary review: morphine-only 23%–48% across 6 series; alcohol 29%–75% across 13, mean 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL; diazepam detected in 12% in one cited series, benzodiazepines 22%, 27%, 55% in 3 others. Correlations −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28. One series: a third below 0.16 mg/L, instant 14%, over 3 h 22%; other series over 2 h 44%, over 3 h 52%; others present 58%–79%. Michigan paper published 1977: 74% no higher than comparison deaths. England/Wales 2000: 1,037; default direct-overdose classification 802/1,037=77.3% and alternatives 235/1,037=22.7% (editors’ calculations); any ceiling/floor interpretation assumes the other assignments were correct and is not a validated bound on true causes or official-statistics errors. Heroin/morphine implicated 424/802, detected 488/802; implicated 42/74 acute events, 33/72 drug-related conditions, 11/18 infections. Alcohol co-detected 316/802=39.4%; methadone implicated 107/802≈13%, sole implicated 4% (sole implication, not sole detection). statement: In nine healthy volunteers in Germany (aged 25 to 48; 2 women and 7 men; how they were recruited or screened is not reported), eating pieces of a poppy-seed cake once (study conditions: 12.5 to 52.3 g of seeds per person, eaten over 10 to 120 minutes), made with the one seed batch, of eight poppy-seed products bought in German supermarkets, health-food shops and a bakery, that held by far the most morphine (151.6 µg per gram of seeds, about 18 to 250 times the 0.6 to 8.4 µg/g of the other seven, editors' arithmetic; a second package of the batch was comparable, other batches of the same maker held 1.1 µg/g), with no control cake and no urine sample from before eating reported, was followed in every volunteer by urinary morphine above 1 µg/mL, the limit for sport that the International Olympic Committee added to its medical code in 1998, measured by GC-MS (Thevis et al., 2003, published as a case report from the Institute of Biochemistry of the German Sport University Cologne; financial support from the Bundesinstitut für Sportwissenschaft, Bonn). Every volunteer was above the limit in at least 2 urine samples (51 of 80 samples, 2 to 8 per person, editors' count), with peaks of 1.93 to 10.04 µg/mL 4 to 11 hours after eating; values above 4 µg/mL, the highest included, were estimated from the calibration curve because such values had not been expected. In eight volunteers the last sample above the limit came 10.25 to 24 hours after eating and the final samples, at 43.75 to 48 hours, held 0.20 to 0.36 µg/mL; one volunteer, whose peak was the highest, was still above the limit at 47.5 hours (1.21 µg/mL), a result the authors concede was shown in only one person after a high amount. All eight products contained morphine and codeine, with codeine negligible in all; urinary codeine was 0.06 to 0.82 µg/mL. The paper judged results only against this sports limit, by GC-MS, without immunoassay screening and without workplace cut-offs, so it cannot show what a workplace drug test would report, and the editors do not apply cut-offs the paper did not use. The morphine each person ate is printed differently in the two tables for every volunteer (1.6 to 6.8 mg in one, 1.8 to 7.7 mg in the other), the cake itself was not analysed, urine dilution was not reported, and the final sample the text dates at 46 to 48 hours appears in the table at 43.75 to 48 hours. A positive here is a urine result, morphine above a limit; effects were not measured. Thebaine, another poppy alkaloid that the authors cite another study as finding in urine after poppy seeds but not after morphine, codeine or street heroin, was not measured, so these results cannot tell poppy seeds apart from heroin or morphine use. The batch was chosen for its unusually high morphine, so the results describe a high-end exposure, not typical poppy-seed foods; the authors' advice that athletes avoid poppy-seed foods before and during competitions goes beyond the data and is not adopted. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Researchers in Germany tested eight poppy-seed products bought in shops and a bakery: all contained some morphine, an opioid, and one batch held far more than the others (about 18 to 250 times as much). They baked that batch into a cake, and nine volunteers each ate some. Every volunteer's urine went above 1 microgram of morphine per millilitre, the limit then used in sports drug testing, in at least two samples. For eight people the last sample above the limit came within a day; one person was still above it about two days later, which the authors say was shown in only one person, after a large amount. The study checked only the sports limit, with one laboratory method; it did not use workplace drug tests, so it cannot say what those would show. A positive here means morphine in urine above a limit; nobody's effects were measured, and the study did not measure what might tell poppy seeds apart from heroin or morphine. There was no comparison cake, no urine sample from before eating, and the seeds were unusually strong, so ordinary poppy-seed foods were not tested.
population: Nine healthy volunteers in Germany, aged 25 to 48 (2 women, 62 and 68 kg; 7 men, 67 to 88 kg); recruitment, screening for opioid or codeine medicines and other poppy-seed foods, and ethics approval not reported
exposure: Poppy-seed cake made with the seed batch holding 151.6 µg of morphine per gram (the highest of eight products bought in Germany; the other seven 0.6 to 8.4 µg/g), eaten once (study conditions: 12.5 to 52.3 g of seeds per person, over 10 to 120 minutes; morphine eaten printed as 1.6 to 6.8 mg in Table II and as 1.8 to 7.7 mg in Table III)
comparator: None: no control cake, no unexposed group and no urine sample from before eating reported; only the course over time within each person
outcome: Total urinary morphine by GC-MS after enzymatic hydrolysis, in urine collected for 24 hours and a final sample at 43.75 to 48 hours, judged against the 1 µg/mL limit of the International Olympic Committee; urinary codeine as a range; morphine content of eight poppy-seed products
magnitude: Thevis et al. (2003), 9 volunteers, 80 urine samples: above 1 µg/mL in 9 of 9 volunteers (Wilson 95% interval 70.1% to 100%, editors' calculation) and in 51 of 80 samples (2 to 8 per volunteer; editors' count); peaks 1.93 to 10.04 µg/mL at 4 to 11 hours (13 values above 4 µg/mL, from 5 volunteers, estimated from the calibration curve); last sample above 1 µg/mL at 10.25 to 24.00 hours in 8 volunteers and at 47.50 hours in 1 (1.21 µg/mL; 1 of 9, 2.0% to 43.5%); final samples of the other 8 at 43.75 to 48.00 hours, 0.20 to 0.36 µg/mL; urinary codeine 0.06 to 0.82 µg/mL. Peaks did not rise steadily with seeds eaten (52.3 g, peak 5.88 µg/mL; 38.1 g, peak 10.04 µg/mL). No comparison condition, so no difference can be given.

risk_of_bias.note: Rated down one level (card: RoB 2, high overall). No control cake, no unexposed group, no urine sample from before eating and no reported screening for codeine medicines or other poppy-seed foods, so the absence of morphine before eating is assumed, not shown; no validation data (limits, calibration range, precision), with the 13 values above 4 µg/mL, the highest included, estimated from the calibration curve; no adjustment for urine dilution, which matters for samples near 1 µg/mL (one volunteer's only two samples above the limit held 1.12 and 1.93 µg/mL); and the morphine eaten differs between the two tables for every volunteer. The rise and fall of morphine after eating in every volunteer makes an outside source unlikely to explain the main finding, so one level, not two.

indirectness.note: Rated down one level. The cake used the one batch, of eight products, with by far the most morphine (151.6 µg/g; the other seven 0.6 to 8.4 µg/g; other batches of the same maker 1.1 µg/g), chosen for that reason, so the results describe a high-end exposure, not typical poppy-seed foods; the products were bought in Germany before October 2001, when the manuscript was received; and results were judged only against a sports limit, by GC-MS, not against workplace screening or confirmation cut-offs. The question is reworded to the sports test.

imprecision.note: Nine volunteers: 9 of 9 above the limit (Wilson 95% interval 70.1% to 100%) and 1 of 9 still above it at about 48 hours (2.0% to 43.5%), editors' calculations.

large_effect.note: A descriptive claim is not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Peaks did not rise steadily with the seeds eaten (the volunteer who ate the most peaked lower than one who ate less).

grade.reasoning: An uncontrolled excretion study in nine volunteers starts low, as a description of what happened after eating this cake (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 (no control and no sample from before eating; unvalidated method with estimated high values; no dilution adjustment; two tables disagreeing on the morphine eaten), indirectness −1 (one unusually morphine-rich batch; a sports limit only) and imprecision −1 (nine people) bring it to very low, the floor. Worded as 'describes', because it reports concentrations after one exposure without a comparison. The paper uses only the sports limit of the time (1 µg/mL, IOC) and GC-MS; it gives no workplace cut-off and no immunoassay result, and the editors do not apply workplace cut-offs the paper does not use. The morphine eaten is given as the range of both tables; the seeds eaten, printed once and consistently, are the study conditions. The authors' general statement about products containing poppy seeds and their advice to athletes are not adopted, because the batch was the most morphine-rich of eight. Thebaine, which the authors cite from another study as a marker of poppy seeds, was not measured, so nothing here tells poppy seeds from heroin or morphine use. Status single study: the authors cite earlier reports of comparable seed contents and urine concentrations, not read here. Funding: the Bundesinstitut für Sportwissenschaft; no conflict-of-interest statement is printed. Amounts appear only as study conditions, and nothing is phrased as advice about tests.

statement: In communities where people who use heroin or other opioids, and others likely to witness an overdose, were trained to recognize and respond to an opioid overdose and given naloxone to take home (an antidote that rapidly reverses the slowed breathing caused by opioids), the programmes are associated with lower opioid overdose death rates after statistical adjustment in the only study that compared death rates with years and places without them (mostly earlier years in the same communities), and most people given naloxone by a trained lay person survived; how many deaths the kits prevented is not known. In 19 Massachusetts cities and towns (Walley et al., 2013), chosen because each had at least five fatal opioid overdoses a year in 2004–2006, just before the programmes began, state-supported programmes of overdose education and nasal naloxone distribution enrolled 2,912 residents from September 2006 to December 2009 (2,007 who reported current drug use, treatment or recovery, and 905 others, typically social-service staff, family and friends), who reported 327 rescue attempts. Yearly opioid overdose death rates for 2002–2009 (poisoning deaths of unintentional or undetermined intent with an opioid-specific code or the narcotic code T40.6 on the death certificate, all opioids together) were compared between community-years with and without enrolment in a Poisson model with one linear time trend. No community had enrolment before 2006 and all 19 had it in 2008 and 2009, so the community-years without enrolment are all 19 communities in 2002–2005 and those not yet enrolling in 2006 and 2007 (12 and 5, by the editors' count): the comparison is mostly of later with earlier years in the same communities, although the introduction speaks of concurrent controls, and no communities outside the 19 were compared. With 1 to 100, and with more than 100 (more than 1 in 1,000 residents), cumulative enrolments per 100,000 residents, the death-rate ratios were 0.93 and 0.82 before adjustment (the editors' reading of a column headed only rate ratio, printed without intervals) and 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91) and 0.54 (0.39 to 0.76) after adjustment for community age, sex, race or ethnicity and poverty, rates of inpatient withdrawal treatment, methadone treatment and state-funded buprenorphine treatment, the share of opioid prescriptions dispensed to people obtaining schedule II opioid prescriptions from four or more prescribers and pharmacies, and year. In the article's second model, by enrolment below or above each year's median, the ratios were 0.85 and 1.00 before and 0.71 (0.57 to 0.90) and 0.78 (0.60 to 1.01) after adjustment, with no gradient, as the authors note; their abstract gives only the first model and calls the programmes an effective intervention, and their interpretation says the effect seemed dose-related. The unadjusted death rates plotted for community-years with enrolment are not consistently lower than those of 2002–2006 (Figure 1, the editors' approximate reading), so the size of the association depends on the adjustment, which includes the time trend. Acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose (emergency-department visits and admissions, analysed together) was not associated with enrolment in either model (adjusted rate ratios 0.90 to 1.00, every interval including 1); the authors suggest that bystanders calling for emergency help, as the training teaches, may balance out fewer overdoses, which was not tested (emergency services were called or present in 106 of 326 reported rescue attempts). The article prints no counts of deaths or hospital visits, no number of community-years in each group and no test for trend, so absolute differences cannot be given; analyses with cut-offs of 75 and 150 enrolments per 100,000, and with opioid overdose deaths divided by cancer deaths, are reported as similar without numbers and without a table (the online supplementary tables, which hold the control models, were not read), and its methods name 75 as the models' cut-off where its results and table use 100. The rescue attempts are trained bystanders' reports, collected when they asked for a naloxone refill: naloxone was reported successful in 150 of the 153 attempts for which this was recorded, the 3 people it did not help received emergency care and survived, and the authors expect that rescues were under-reported. The authors state that their observational study cannot prove that the programmes caused the reduction (Walley et al., 2013). The study was funded by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with the first author as principal investigator and no role for the funder; the first author is listed as medical director of the Massachusetts opioid overdose prevention pilot, the trainers worked under a standing order from the programme's medical director, and three of the eight authors list the Massachusetts Department of Public Health, which expanded the programme and kept the programme database used for the enrolment counts; the competing-interests statement, which covers the previous three years, does not mention these roles. A systematic review of 22 observational studies published to June 2015 (McDonald & Strang, 2016: 15 in the USA, 2 in Canada, 4 in the UK and 1 in the UK and Germany; none randomized, two with a comparison group; eligibility, data extraction and quality rating by the first author under the supervision of the senior investigator), which includes the Massachusetts study, counted 2,336 naloxone administrations by trained lay people in 17 studies, after which 20 people were confirmed dead (0.9%), and at least 2,249 (96.3%) survived when 4 deaths with unclear naloxone use and 63 unknown outcomes are also counted as failures. These reversals, as the review calls them, count survival after naloxone, not deaths prevented: the review uses them as a stand-in because it cannot tell which overdoses would have been fatal without naloxone, and it cites a ratio of one fatal overdose in every 20 overdoses (editors' calculation: at that ratio, about 117 of 2,336 overdoses would have been expected to end in death; overdoses in which naloxone was used may have been more severe than most, so this only shows that survivals are not deaths prevented). In 21 of the 22 studies the overdose outcomes rested only on what participants reported, and in the 10 studies with unsystematic follow-up only 1,973 of 8,602 recipients (22.9%) are recorded as returning for a refill after using naloxone. The review judged that take-home naloxone met all nine Bradford Hill criteria for causation, but its own results call the dose–response criterion only partly met and give the experimental-evidence criterion only preliminary support, both resting on the Massachusetts study alone, which is also the only included study that used death records; strength of association, biological plausibility and coherence rest on survival counts from 21 studies, consistency on reversals in at least 15 places, specificity on two cases, analogy on other emergency treatments given by lay people, and temporality on 21 studies in which training preceded reversals, among which the review singles out the Massachusetts study and an uncontrolled programme report from Chicago (fatal overdoses fell 20%, 8% and 6% in 2001–2003 after a 135% rise in 1996–2000), from which it says no definite conclusion can be drawn. The review describes the Massachusetts result as a fall compared with rates before implementation and with communities without the programme, and calls its dose relationship significant; in the full article, community-years without the programme exist only up to 2007, a gradient appears in only one of its two models, and no test for trend is printed. The review's abstract gives one death in 123 overdoses (0.8%, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2) without saying that the figure comes from the nine studies with systematic follow-up, and the printed interval fits a denominator of 2,336, not 123 (editors' calculation: exact interval about 0.02% to 4.4%). The review notes that critics argue the observational data are not strong enough to infer that naloxone provision reduces deaths, and that overdose deaths in Australia fell during a heroin shortage in 2001–2002, before take-home naloxone was introduced there. Both review authors' employer holds intellectual property on a naloxone formulation, the second author (Strang) declares funding and payments from pharmaceutical companies, including work on naloxone products, and a patent registration for another naloxone formulation, and he co-wrote two of the included studies. Which drugs: all 22 studies reported mainly heroin overdoses, methadone was involved in fewer than 5% of reversals in the one study that reported it, and the review states that its results are limited to heroin overdoses and that effectiveness for long-acting opioids such as methadone or many prescription opioids is unclear; the Massachusetts deaths are counted for all opioids together, not by drug; neither source mentions fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In 19 Massachusetts cities and towns with many opioid overdose deaths, programmes trained 2,912 people from 2006 to 2009 to respond to an overdose and gave out nasal naloxone, the antidote to heroin and other opioids. Once more than 1 in 1,000 residents had been trained, opioid overdose death rates were about half those of years without training, after allowing for other differences, but only about a fifth lower, it seems, before allowing for them. Because every town had the programme by 2008, that comparison is mostly with earlier years in the same towns; another way of grouping the towns showed no extra drop where more people were trained, hospital visits for overdose showed no link, and the study printed no death counts. It could not show cause. A review of 22 studies, mostly programme reports, found that after trained people gave naloxone 2,336 times, 20 people were known to have died. That shows survival after naloxone, not how many lives it saved, because most overdoses do not end in death: the review cites about 1 death in every 20 overdoses. Most of the overdoses in the review's studies were from heroin; the Massachusetts deaths were not broken down by drug, and none of the studies looked at fentanyl separately.

risk_of_bias.note: Massachusetts study (card sc_walley_2013, ROBINS-I serious, now judged from the full article; first-pass): confounding. Roll-out was not random, and the communities were chosen for high mortality just before the programmes began, so some fall was expected; all 19 communities had the programme in 2008–2009, so the community-years without it are mostly 2002–2005 and the contrast rests largely on later against earlier years through one linear time trend, with no comparison communities, community-specific trends, or measures of other prevention activity or the drug supply; the association is much weaker before adjustment (0.93 and 0.82; in the second model 0.85 and 1.00), and the unadjusted rates plotted for community-years with enrolment are not consistently lower than in 2002–2006. Review (card sc_mcdonald_2016, AMSTAR 2 critically low, provisional): the survival counts have no comparison, rest on self-report in 21 of 22 studies and on unsystematic follow-up in 10, and were pooled without weighting.

inconsistency.note: Only one study compared death rates with a comparison (an uncontrolled Chicago programme report, as the review summarizes it, also describes falling deaths). Within it, the absolute model shows lower adjusted rates in both strata and the relative model in the below-median stratum only (above the median 0.78, 0.60 to 1.01); this dependence on the model is counted under risk of bias, not as inconsistency between studies. The survival counts point the same way across 17 studies but measure a different thing, so there is nothing to compare for inconsistency.

indirectness.note: Survival after naloxone, the review's main outcome, is a stand-in for deaths prevented, which it cannot measure; the death-rate evidence comes from one US state in 2002–2009 and counts deaths with any opioid code together, not by drug; the review's studies concern mainly heroin overdoses and its authors say effectiveness for long-acting opioids such as methadone or many prescription opioids is unclear; neither source mentions fentanyl, so the answer is indirect for fentanyl and for today's drug supply.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: the adjusted intervals exclude no difference in three of the four strata (0.57 to 0.91; 0.39 to 0.76; 0.57 to 0.90) and reach 1.01 in the fourth; their width and overlap leave the size of any effect uncertain, the crude ratios carry no intervals, and the instability across models is counted under risk of bias.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: the review checked only the grey literature, a search it calls probably not exhaustive.

large_effect.note: Not applied: 0.54 is not below 0.5, the crude ratio for that stratum is 0.82, the second model gives 0.71 and 0.78, and bias left after adjustment could run either way.

dose_response.note: Not applied: a gradient appears only in the absolute model, whose two strata have overlapping intervals, with no test for trend printed; in the relative model the above-median stratum had the weaker association (0.78 against 0.71), and the authors say there did not seem to be a dose relation in that model (the review calls the dose relationship significant, second-hand); the evidence is also already rated down for risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (an ecological time series in which most of the comparison is of later with earlier years in the same communities, through one linear time trend, and whose association is much weaker before adjustment; and survival counts without comparison) and one for indirectness (survival after naloxone stands in for deaths prevented; heroin, not fentanyl): very low. Rated as worded: an association between programme roll-out and lower opioid overdose death rates in one US state, and survival after naloxone given by trained lay people; the claim does not say that the kits prevented any number of deaths, which no study read could measure. Revisited after the full article of Walley et al. (2013) was read (the earlier versions rested on the BMJ's one-page print summary): the rating stays very low. The full article adds that all 19 communities had the programme in 2008–2009, that its second exposure model shows no gradient, that the unadjusted death rates it plots are not consistently lower with enrolment, that acute hospital care showed no association, and that no death counts are printed; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down two levels for the death-rate evidence, which would leave the certainty at very low, the lowest level. Overlap: the review includes the Massachusetts study, on which its dose–response and experimental-evidence judgments and its community-level mortality conclusion rest entirely, so the two sources are not independent for deaths. The review's other studies support that trained lay people used naloxone and that most people given it survived, not how many deaths were prevented; its judgment that all nine Bradford Hill criteria are met is reported as its judgment, with its own qualifications (dose–response only partly met, experimental evidence preliminary). Its abstract interval for one death in 123 is not used as printed (editors' recalculation in the statement). 'Is associated with', not 'reduces', at very low certainty (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: only one study compared death rates with a comparison. A review of fatal heroin overdoses in Victoria, Australia, listed in the project's harm-reduction list as a counter-case to take-home naloxone (Stam et al., 2018), is not on file; read it before this claim leaves draft.

statement: In the City of Vancouver, Canada, in 2001–2005, the opening of North America's first medically supervised injection site (the supervised injecting facility in the Downtown Eastside, opened on 21 September 2003, where people inject drugs obtained beforehand under the supervision of health professionals who give emergency care, including oxygen and naloxone; by an earlier count, heroin made up about 40% of the injections there, powder cocaine about 30% and methamphetamine 5%) is associated with a larger fall in coroner-recorded overdose deaths within 500 metres of the site than in the rest of the city, in one before-and-after study without adjustment for anything else. Within 500 metres there were 56 deaths in the 2.7 years before the opening (22,066 person-years; 253.8 per 100,000 person-years, 95% CI 187.3 to 320.3) and 33 in the 2.3 years after (19,991 person-years; 165.1, 108.8 to 221.4), a fall of 35.0% (0.0% to 57.7%; rate difference 88.7 per 100,000 person-years, 1.6 to 175.8, p=0.048), about 6 fewer deaths a year (editors' calculation: about 20.6 a year before and 14.5 after); in the rest of the city there were 113 deaths (1,479,792 person-years; 7.6 per 100,000) and 88 (1,271,246; 6.9), a fall of 9.3% (−19.8% to 31.4%; p=0.490). The test of the difference between the two falls in absolute terms (rate differences; Breslow-Day) gave p=0.049, which the summary calls a significant interaction and the results describe as heterogeneity that might be present; the relative falls (rate ratios 0.65 and 0.91) do not differ significantly (p about 0.20; editors' calculations). The rates rest on census populations interpolated between 2001 and 2006: the population of city blocks within 500 metres rose 14% from 2001 to 2005, which the authors link to more supportive housing, and with the population held at its 2001 level the fall near the site was 30% and not statistically significant (no interval or p value given), although a block-by-block test still showed an overall fall with either population (15 of 22 blocks with deaths fell; p=0.039 both ways). In census tracts, falls were larger nearer the site, minimal beyond about 500 metres and negligible beyond 1 km. Deaths were counted by the place of death, not by use of the site, and no individual was followed (Marshall et al., 2011, a retrospective population-based study of all 290 deaths ruled accidental illicit drug overdoses by the British Columbia Coroners Service, 89 of them, 30.7%, within 500 metres and 201 farther away). The coroners recorded opioids as contributing to 156 of the 290 deaths and cocaine to 175 (editors' sums from Table 1; a death can involve both), with no significant change in the drugs involved in either area; the paper does not mention fentanyl. The authors could not adjust for neighbourhood changes because Statistics Canada suppressed area characteristics; they report no evidence of changes in drug supply or purity, drug-use patterns, methadone treatment, policing or migration, partly from other studies; one spike of deaths from stolen powdered methadone, after the opening; and police referral of people injecting in public to the site throughout; they state that confounding by unmeasured factors cannot be excluded and that the area-level design calls for caution. High overdose mortality in Vancouver in the 1990s led to the site's opening in the Downtown Eastside; it had 12 injection seats, over 500 supervised injections a day and about 5,000 people who inject drugs nearby, and an earlier study had recorded no deaths inside it. The authors (funded by Vancouver Coastal Health, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research; three of the five also wrote earlier reports of the site's evaluation, which was first funded by Health Canada) call such facilities safe and effective in the discussion, and conclude that they should be considered for assessment where injection drug use is prevalent. A published letter (Christian et al., 2012) argues that the decline owes much to starting in 2001, a year in which, it says, heroin was far more available and deaths more common than in any later year, and that police added in 2003 to 12 city blocks around the site, where it says most of the deaths behind the fall lay (48 to 66 officers, still deployed when it wrote, by an unnamed personal communication), are the most likely cause of any real fall; its own data are yearly death counts, not rates, plotted without values for British Columbia, Vancouver and the Downtown Eastside, all larger areas than the study's (editors' reading of the plot, approximate: Vancouver about 89 deaths in 2001, 49 in 2002 and 56 in 2005; the Downtown Eastside about 31, 27 and 37 in the same years). Neither of the two papers it cites that are on file measured heroin availability or purity (Kerr et al., 2007, cited for the 2001 point; Wood et al., 2004, cited for policing); its other source on heroin, a 2006 paper by three of the study's authors on Canadian heroin supply, which it dates 2004, is not on file. The authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012) answers that the letter's Downtown Eastside figures cover the whole local health area (about 400 city blocks, against the study's 41) and, by its account, all drug-induced deaths, suicides included, as counts rather than rates; cites the team's own reports that daily heroin use stayed stable from 2001 to 2005, and a police evaluation for the crackdown having ended within weeks of the opening, so that any displacement would, it argues, have lowered deaths near the site before the opening; and reports a fall of 36% among the deaths with signs of injection at the scene (85% of the 89 near the site), with no count, interval or comparison area; it does not reanalyse the study from 2002, answer the fall in reported non-fatal overdoses that the letter cites from the team's earlier work (Kerr et al., 2007), or give the share of deaths without signs of injection in the rest of the city. The two cited papers on file describe the background; neither reports overdose deaths. In a Vancouver cohort of 1,587 people who inject drugs, enrolled from 1996 to 2004 and interviewed every 6 months (12,030 interviews), the yearly share who reported a non-fatal overdose of any drug in the previous 6 months (12 months, by the letter) was 21% in 1997 and 6% in 2004, with the largest step between about 12% in 2001 and about 5% in 2002, before the site opened, and about 5% to 7% from 2002 to 2004 (read from a figure, approximate; yearly denominators not printed; the figures are not broken down by area); its authors suggest that reduced heroin supply may have played a role and that expanded methadone treatment may also be involved (the letter says they clearly point to supply), had no measure of supply and could not take drug purity into account (Kerr et al., 2007). The study's before period began on 1 January 2001 and so includes that higher year, as does its comparison with the rest of the city. The police crackdown in the Downtown Eastside began on 7 April 2003, inside the before period; in its first three months, discarded syringes fell within a block of Main and Hastings (monthly averages 1,082 to 585) and rose in the rest of the Downtown Eastside (784 to 1,253), the only area counted (the letter places the rise in other areas of Vancouver), more cohort members living there said police had changed where they used drugs, and reported daily heroin use and heroin prices did not differ detectably; the paper does not say how long the crackdown lasted (Wood et al., 2004). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In Vancouver, Canada, coroners recorded 290 deaths from overdoses of illegal drugs from 2001 to 2005; about half involved opioids and about 6 in 10 cocaine. Within 500 metres of the city's supervised injection site, where people inject heroin, cocaine and other drugs under the eye of health workers, deaths went from 56 in the 2¾ years before it opened in September 2003 to 33 in the 2¼ years after: the death rate fell by about a third, against about 1 in 10 in the rest of the city, which could be chance, and the gap between these two falls could be chance too. The study compared only before and after, allowed for nothing else that changed, such as more housing nearby, and counted deaths by where they happened, not by who used the site. When the area's population was taken as unchanged, the fall near the site was 30 in 100 and could be chance. In a published letter, critics said the fall came from extra police around the site and from starting the count in 2001, a year with unusually many deaths and, they said, more heroin around; their own counts covered much bigger areas, and their police figures came from an unnamed source. The authors replied that the police crackdown ended within weeks of the opening, and that among deaths with signs of injecting the rate still fell 36 in 100; neither side re-ran the study's numbers from 2002. Neither of the two papers the critics cited that we have read measured how much heroin there was or how strong it was. In one, a study of 1,587 people who inject drugs in Vancouver, the share who said they had overdosed in the past 6 months fell from about 21 in 100 in 1997 to about 6 in 100 in 2004, with the biggest drop between 2001 (about 12 in 100) and 2002 (about 5 in 100), before the site opened; its authors suggested less heroin and more methadone treatment as possible reasons. The other dates the police crackdown from April 2003, months before the opening: in its first three months, drug use seemed to move to nearby streets of the same neighbourhood; it counted no deaths and does not say how long the crackdown lasted. The main study does not mention fentanyl.
population: Residents of the City of Vancouver as the denominator (census populations; on average about 8,100 before and 8,800 after within 500 metres of the site, editors' calculation from person-years), with the 290 deaths ruled accidental illicit drug overdoses by the British Columbia Coroners Service from 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2005 (229 men; median age 40), counted by place of death; the site's neighbourhood, the Downtown Eastside, had about 5,000 people who inject drugs, as cited
exposure: Place of death within 500 metres of North America's first medically supervised injection site (all census blocks whose centre lay within 500 metres, fixed in advance because over 70% of daily clients in a random sample lived within that distance), after its opening on 21 September 2003 (to 31 December 2005); no individual measure of use of the site
comparator: The same area before the opening (1 January 2001 to 20 September 2003), and the rest of the city over the same two periods; no adjustment for other factors
outcome: Rate of coroner-ruled accidental illicit drug overdose deaths per 100,000 person-years (census populations interpolated between 2001 and 2006), compared as rate differences and percentage falls, with a Breslow-Day test of the difference between areas

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_marshall_2011 (ROBINS-I, first pass): serious, from confounding. An unadjusted comparison of two periods with no earlier trend, in an area chosen for its high overdose mortality; changes in the same area over the same years (more supportive housing and a 14% rise in population, police referral of people injecting in public to the site) are bundled with the opening, and others (supply, treatment, migration) are argued from other studies or measured only among the site's clients; deaths are placed by where they happened, not by who used the site. The outcome data are strong (all coroner-ruled deaths, unchanged criteria) and the 500 m radius was fixed in advance. A published letter adds a police operation around the site in 2003 and a fall in heroin supply around 2001 as changes at the same time, the first resting on an unnamed personal communication and the second on a cohort's self-reported overdoses and a paper not on file; the authors' reply cites a police evaluation for the operation having ended within weeks and its own reports of stable daily heroin use (Christian et al., 2012; Marshall et al., 2012). The two cited papers on file measured neither heroin availability or purity nor overdose deaths: they show a fall in self-reported non-fatal overdoses in a Vancouver cohort, largest between 2001 and 2002, inside the before period (Kerr et al., 2007), and a police crackdown in the Downtown Eastside from April 2003, also inside the before period, after which more people living there reported changing where they used drugs and discarded syringes shifted within the neighbourhood (Wood et al., 2004). None of this changes the judgment, which already rests on unmeasured changes at the same time.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for one site, its 500 m area and 2001–2005, with the drugs named as the coroners recorded them; it does not say how sites elsewhere, or a drug supply with fentanyl, would compare, which the paper does not address.

imprecision.note: 56 and 33 deaths near the site; the interval for the 35% fall reaches 0.0%, the test of the difference between the two areas' absolute falls gives p=0.049 (their relative falls do not differ significantly, p about 0.20, editors' calculation), and with the population held at its 2001 level the fall (30%) is not statistically significant.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study; the authors' search found no other peer-reviewed study of a site's effect on overdose deaths up to December 2009.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the rate ratio near the site (0.65, editors' calculation) is not below 0.5, and the comparison is unadjusted.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the larger falls in census tracts nearer the site come from an exploratory fit, and the evidence is already rated down for risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (an unadjusted before-and-after comparison with changes at the same time) and one for imprecision (few deaths, an interval reaching no fall, a borderline difference between the areas in absolute falls only, and a fall near the site that loses significance when the population is held constant): very low. Rated as worded: an association between the opening of one site and a larger fall in coroner-recorded overdose deaths within 500 m than elsewhere in Vancouver in 2001–2005; not that supervised injection sites reduce deaths, nor that people who used the site were less likely to die, which the study did not measure. The authors' discussion calls such facilities safe and effective; 'safe' rests on other studies they cite, not on these data, and their conclusion asks that sites be considered for assessment. The drugs: opioids contributed to about half of the deaths and cocaine to about 6 in 10 (editors' sums; a death can involve both), and people at the site injected mostly heroin and powder cocaine; the paper does not mention fentanyl, so it says nothing about a supply in which fentanyl is common. Status single study. Now read against the published letter (Christian et al., 2012) and the authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012), from their PDFs (METHODS §2.3): rating and status unchanged. The letter disputes the cause of the fall, which the claim does not assert, and names two further changes at the same time (a police operation around the site in 2003 and a fall in heroin supply around 2001), now in the statement; it is entered as argument, attributed, since its own data are counts for areas larger than the study's, its police figures rest on an unnamed personal communication and its other figures are second-hand. The study's comparison with the rest of the city shares the 2001 start, and in the letter's own figure the drop from 2001 to 2002 is large in the Vancouver series (about 89 to 49 deaths) and small in the Downtown Eastside series (about 31 to 27; editors' reading). The reply answers the points on area, kinds of death and rates, and adds one restricted reanalysis of the same records (36%, no interval or comparison area), which is not independent replication; its answers on heroin and policing rest on its authors' own reports and a police evaluation, not read here; it leaves the 2001 start, the non-fatal overdose trend and the share of deaths without signs of injection elsewhere unanswered; and its call for such facilities to be central to responses goes beyond the paper's own call for assessment. Which deaths the letter's Downtown Eastside series counts cannot be settled from the two letters (a coroners' publication on illicit drug deaths, by the letter; vital statistics including suicides, by the reply). Also read against the two papers the letter cites that are on file (Kerr et al., 2007; Wood et al., 2004), from their PDFs: rating and status unchanged. Neither measured heroin availability or purity or overdose deaths, and neither reports figures for the study's two areas (within 500 m of the site and the rest of the city), so neither tests the letter's explanations or the study's association. The cohort's fall in self-reported non-fatal overdoses, largest between 2001 and 2002, is a fact about the background in the study's before period, which began in 2001: it fits the letter's point that 2001 was a high year in that cohort, but the study's comparison with the rest of the city shares the same start, the cohort is not split by area, and its authors' reasons (heroin supply, methadone) are suggestions without data on supply. The crackdown began inside the before period, and in its first three months more people living in the Downtown Eastside reported changing where they used drugs and discarded syringes shifted from its core to the rest of the neighbourhood; whether added police stayed after the opening (the letter) or left within weeks of it (the reply), neither paper shows. The letter departs from both papers in places: the cohort's question covered 6 months, not 12; its authors offer reduced supply only as a possible reason, alongside methadone; and the syringe counts that rose were in the rest of the Downtown Eastside, the only area counted, not in other areas of Vancouver (the paper's own abstract speaks of displacement into adjacent areas of the city). Not contested (§6.4): the letter offers no reanalysis of the study's areas and does not change the reading of the claim as worded, an unadjusted association near one site. Later evaluations of the same site, on the project's PDF request list, and the letter's other source on heroin (a 2006 paper by three of the study's authors on Canadian heroin supply, dated 2004 in the letter, which the study itself cites for stable drug use) are not on file; the claim must still be read against them before it leaves draft (METHODS §2.3).

statement: In people who take loperamide to manage opioid withdrawal, evidence is insufficient to say whether loperamide, compared with no loperamide or with withdrawal medicines, relieves withdrawal symptoms: the one study read, a US registry of 26 people seen by medical toxicologists after loperamide exposure (2010 or 2011 to 2016), recorded that 6 of them had taken it to avoid withdrawal, but it recorded only the problems that brought people to care, not whether their withdrawal eased, and it has no comparison group. Its authors write that people use loperamide to relieve withdrawal themselves and that a lack of methadone or buprenorphine treatment may play a part, which the study did not measure. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: No study we read measured whether loperamide eases opioid withdrawal. The one study recorded only the heart and breathing problems of people who became ill after taking it, six of whom had taken it for withdrawal.
population: People who take loperamide to avoid or relieve opioid withdrawal (6 of 26 registry cases seen by US medical toxicologists)
comparator: No loperamide, or withdrawal medicines (no data)
magnitude: No data: relief of withdrawal was not recorded. 6 of the 12 misuse cases (26 in all) had taken loperamide to avoid withdrawal; their outcomes are not reported separately.
